common_context: Qwen3-8B code-execution paper reader, 35 replay-verified trajectories; in a 40-question development comparison errors fell 22 to 1 but provisional supported answers on 20 answerable questions stayed 3 for base and v5; small compute/annotation budget.

cases.question: More supervised examples or another small GRPO run?

A.recommendation: Invest the next annotation effort in targeted, manually corrected supervised examples, while deferring all training until supported-answer labels and a held-out comparison exist. Do not schedule another GRPO run now.
A.baseline: The existing 35 replay-verified trajectories and v5 SFT checkpoint; retain the current no-training policy.
A.matched_test: Without GPU, independently review the 20 answerable development cases, categorize unsupported answers and execution faults, and draft/replay corrections for distinct answer-support failures. Before any later training, hold out named questions and compare an equal-compute corrected-example SFT run with a GRPO run only if a semantic reward can be validated.
A.decision_rule: Training threshold explicitly unset until named held-out tasks and independent human support judgments exist. Proceed to GRPO only after its reward agrees with human support judgments on a prespecified validation set; agreement threshold currently unset.
A.uncertainty: The cited studies concern math, software tasks, and medical multiple choice, not this paper reader. The 3/20 provisional answer result has not been independently reviewed. SFT can overfit small demonstrations.

claims.text: The SRL authors caution that SFT on modest sets of long demonstrations may overfit and report that both SFT and outcome-based RL struggle on challenging tasks.
Med-RLVR uses an outcome correctness and format verifier for its medical multiple-choice reward.

B.recommendation: Spend the next scarce budget on human review of answer support and a small number of failure-targeted, verified supervised trajectories; defer another GRPO run. This is a priority for evidence collection and data curation, not a claim that adding examples will necessarily improve the model.
B.baseline: Before training, compare the current v5 checkpoint with the same checkpoint given a compact, fixed few-shot prompt containing reviewed tool-use-and-evidence demonstrations. Keep the question set, corpus, decoding, and scoring identical; exclude test-question content from demonstrations.
B.matched_test: On the same frozen 40 development questions, blindly review answer support for the 20 answerable items, and record execution-error episodes, latency, and inference cost for all 40. Compare current v5 with the no-training few-shot baseline using paired question-level results. Reserve separate, unseen questions before any later SFT model is promoted; do not call the 40-question development result a held-out effect, or treat source span presence or replay success as answer correctness.
B.decision_rule: Predeclared development-pilot gate, not a significance claim: prioritize preparing a small targeted SFT dataset if the reviewed few-shot baseline improves supported-answer passes from v5’s 3/20 to at least 6/20 on the same answerable development items, loses none of the three currently passing items, keeps execution-error episodes at or below 1/40, and keeps median latency and inference cost each at or below 1.20× v5. Train when compute exists, then require a separately reserved matched held-out test before claiming model improvement. Reconsider GRPO only after a blinded audit shows a reliable reward that tracks supported-answer judgments on unseen outputs and a small matched rollout shows nontrivial reward variation; the numerical agreement/variation threshold for that future GRPO gate is explicitly unset pending labeled samples.
B.uncertainty: The 3/20 supported-answer counts are provisional, the sample is small, and no causal comparison of additional SFT versus GRPO exists for this specific Qwen3-8B reader. The cited math/tool-RL studies use different tasks, model scales, and verifiable ground-truth rewards, so their gains do not transfer directly. The proposed +3/20 threshold is a practical pilot rule rather than a statistical confidence bound.

claims.text: DeepSeekMath GRPO replaces PPO’s learned value-model baseline with scores from multiple outputs to the same question.
DeepSeekMath’s reported RL phase used about 144,000 math questions and sampled 64 outputs per question.
ReTool trained a code-integrated cold-start SFT model before applying RL with interleaved code execution.
ReTool used a rule-based final-answer correctness reward against ground truth and did not include code executability in that reward.
DeepSeek-R1’s authors say reward reliability is central to RL and that reliable signals are hard to construct for open-ended tasks.
DeepSeek-R1’s authors report reward hacking with a helpfulness reward: reward rose while Codeforces performance fell.

cases.question: BM25 alone or hybrid retrieval plus reranking for long research papers?

A.recommendation: Keep BM25 as the production baseline and test BM25 plus dense rank fusion. Treat reranking as a separate ablation, not part of the default candidate.
A.baseline: Current BM25 passage search with the same segmentation and passage budget.
A.matched_test: On identical long-paper questions and cached passages, compare BM25, BM25+dense fusion, then fusion+reranker. Blindly assess whether answer-support spans enter the top-k and whether the fixed reader gives supported answers; measure local indexing, retrieval, and end-to-end latency.
A.decision_rule: Promote hybrid only if it recovers at least 3 more support spans among 40 questions and loses no more than 1 span found by BM25, with no decrease in independently reviewed supported answers. Reranker must improve at least 2 additional support-span hits beyond hybrid; latency ceiling unset pending hardware measurement.
A.uncertainty: SciRet uses CORD-19 with pseudo-relevance labels, so its retrieval scores are not a QASPER prediction. A generic cross-encoder may reduce precision in this domain; paper-specific retrieval and reranking costs are unknown.

claims.text: SciRet reports hybrid BM25 plus dense recall gains in its scientific corpus, while an MS MARCO cross-encoder reduced precision in its tested setup.
Lit3R combines sparse and dense retrieval with reranking for literature-grounded QA.

B.recommendation: Keep BM25 as the shipping baseline and run an offline hybrid BM25+dense candidate test; add reranking only as a separately measured ablation, because domain mismatch can hurt.
B.baseline: Existing BM25 passage ranking, fixed passage segmentation and top-k/token budget.
B.matched_test: Use the same frozen papers/questions and human evidence sets. Compare BM25, BM25+dense fusion, and fusion+reranker at identical top-k and downstream context token budget; record full-evidence-set recall, answer support, per-query retrieval latency, index size, and memory.
B.decision_rule: Pilot only if hybrid improves complete human-evidence-set hit by at least 3 questions on 20 answerable cases, with no decrease in human-reviewed supported answers and retrieval p95 latency no more than 25% above BM25. Admit reranking only if it adds at least 2 further complete evidence hits without losing supported answers. Thresholds are local pilot choices.
B.uncertainty: The available studies use different corpora and models; SciRet labels risk favoring the hybrid system. Local evidence-hit and latency baselines are unset, so no production switch is justified yet.

claims.text: QASPER pairs full research papers with human-selected supporting evidence, allowing evidence retrieval to be evaluated separately from answer generation.
SciRet found hybrid retrieval more robust than sparse or dense alone in its scientific corpus, but its pseudo-relevance labels were derived from the hybrid system.
SciRet reported that an MS MARCO-trained cross-encoder reduced precision on its scientific corpus.
A QASPER study examined a retriever-ranker-reader pipeline and reported that stage choices affected answer quality.

cases.question: Prefix caching or speculative decoding for two concurrent Qwen3-8B readers?

A.recommendation: Test prefix caching first if the two readers reuse an identical serialized system/paper prefix; make prompt-prefix identity and cache-hit rate the first measurements. If real traffic shares little prefix or decode dominates, test speculative decoding next.
A.baseline: Same Qwen3-8B serving stack with prefix caching disabled and speculative decoding disabled, two concurrent clients, frozen prompt and output-length distribution.
A.matched_test: On the same machine and two-client replay, alternate caching off/on after warmup with the same exact prompt bytes and decoding settings. Include a shared-prefix stratum and a deliberately distinct-prefix stratum. Record TTFT, inter-token latency, end-to-end p50/p95, output tokens, throughput, VRAM, and cache hits.
A.decision_rule: Pursue prefix caching if the shared-prefix stratum yields at least 20% lower median TTFT and at least 10% lower median end-to-end latency, with p95 end-to-end no worse than 10%, and the real workload exhibits at least 50% prefix reuse. Otherwise test speculative decoding under the same two-client load. These are predeclared local thresholds.
A.uncertainty: Actual prompt serialization, prefix overlap, prefill/decode split, hardware, and baseline latency are unset. Prefix caching offers no expected benefit for divergent prefixes; no speedup is assumed.

claims.text: vLLM prefix caching reuses KV cache for matching prefixes and reduces prefill work, but it does not reduce decoding time.
vLLM documents speculative decoding primarily as a way to reduce inter-token latency for medium-to-low-QPS, memory-bound workloads.
A serving study found speculative-decoding speedups often shrink as server load rises and depend on draft acceptance and model sizes.

B.recommendation: Measure prefix reuse and prefix caching first for two concurrent readers; defer speculative decoding until output decode time is shown to dominate.
B.baseline: Current two-reader serving configuration with cache disabled or cold prefixes, same model, prompts, decoding, and concurrency.
B.matched_test: Replay the same two-reader paired workload with prefix cache off and on, alternating order and logging shared-token fraction, time to first token, decode tokens per second, end-to-end p50/p95 latency, KV memory, and cache-hit rate. Include short and long outputs.
B.decision_rule: Keep caching only if warm-cache end-to-end p50 falls by at least 10% without p95 or answer-quality regression; mark the result inconclusive if shared-prefix hit rate is low. The acceptable KV-memory increase is explicitly unset until measured.
B.uncertainty: The prefix-caching paper uses larger multi-agent workflows and up to H100 class hardware; speculative decoding results depend on a useful draft model. Neither directly measures two Qwen3-8B readers.

claims.text: KVFlow reports that its prefix-cache gains shrink as outputs grow because decoding dominates runtime.
Speculative decoding targets serial autoregressive decode steps by drafting and verifying multiple tokens in parallel.

cases.question: Entire long paper or iterative selected-passage inspection for paper QA?

A.recommendation: Use iterative search and inspection of selected passages, with explicit evidence coverage checks and a fallback to broader paper inspection on uncertain or multi-hop cases.
A.baseline: One pass supplying the whole available paper text to the same reader and answer prompt, within an equalized context budget.
A.matched_test: On the same 40 questions, compare full-paper input with bounded iterative search/read at equal model and output limits. Independently mark required evidence spans, supported-answer quality, missed-evidence cases, input tokens, latency, and execution errors.
A.decision_rule: Adopt selected-passage reading if independently reviewed supported-answer passes are no lower than full-paper, missed required evidence increases by at most 1/40, and median input tokens fall by at least 25%. Treat small sample uncertainty explicitly.
A.uncertainty: The QASPER discourse study tested different models and a structured retriever; selected passages can omit global or multi-hop context. The project question set is a development comparison, not a held-out leaderboard.

claims.text: On QASPER evidence retrieval, the D3 authors report 99.6% of their best zero-shot baseline performance using 26% of its tokens.
The FinanceBench paper identifies missed relevant pages or chunks despite finding the correct long document.

B.recommendation: Keep iterative search and inspection of selected passages as the default paper-reading path, with a bounded ability to inspect neighboring sections and revisit search; test whole-paper input as a matched comparator on papers that fit context.
B.baseline: One whole-paper prompt with the same model, decoding, question, source text normalization, and maximum total input/output token cap wherever the paper fits.
B.matched_test: Replay the same answerable and unanswerable questions through whole-paper input and the current iterative search/read/extract path. For papers exceeding the limit, report a separate infeasible stratum rather than truncating silently. Blind-review atomic answer support, completeness, tool failures, tokens, and latency.
B.decision_rule: Retain iterative inspection if it yields at least 3 more supported answers on 20 answerable cases, or equal support with at least 25% fewer total input tokens, and does not add more than 1 execution-error episode on 40. Whole-paper wins only if it improves supported answers by at least 3 and fits at least 90% of the selected paper set within the configured context cap. These are pilot thresholds.
B.uncertainty: The studies are not a direct Qwen3-8B code-reader comparison. Retrieval misses, multi-section synthesis, and paper-length distribution may overturn the default; local token and latency measurements are unset.

claims.text: Long-context model performance can degrade when relevant information sits in the middle of a long input.
A QASPER document-QA system explicitly separated text extraction, evidence retrieval, and answer generation and reported a 7.19 Answer-F1 gain over its baselines.
LongRAG argues that passage chunking can lose global context and noisy retrieval can obscure evidence, motivating some access to broader structure.

cases.question: Teacher-generated trajectories or manually corrected failures when 100 more can be reviewed?

A.recommendation: Prioritize manual correction of the reader’s own failed trajectories, especially unsupported answers with successful execution; retain the original failing prefix and add a verified recovery continuation. Use teacher traces only where they cover an unmet failure class and pass human evidence checks.
A.baseline: Unfiltered teacher-generated successful traces, with a human verifying tool execution and answer evidence before any use.
A.matched_test: Use the 100-review budget on 50 reader failure cases and 50 teacher traces sampled from the same question/failure strata. Blindly score each for a novel, replayable, evidence-supported action/answer correction and annotation minutes. No training is required for this screening. If training later becomes available, compare equal-count SFT sets on frozen held-out questions.
A.decision_rule: Allocate subsequent annotation to corrected failures if at least 10 more of the 50 are novel, replayable, evidence-supported learning examples than the teacher arm, or if yield per annotation hour is at least 25% higher, with no increased rate of unsupported final answers in a later matched SFT test. These are local pilot thresholds.
A.uncertainty: No direct head-to-head study on this reader exists. Manual correction may be slow and can introduce annotator inconsistency; teacher traces may help novel tool paths. The cited correction studies concern different models/tasks and do not establish a local effect size.

claims.text: ROSS argues historical rollouts contain mistakes and redundant actions that should not all be imitated, and applies supervision selectively.
Reflective Recovery turns failed prefixes into recovery examples and reports gains on mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
SCoRe found offline supervised correction traces can suffer distribution mismatch and behavior collapse, so corrected traces are not guaranteed to teach recovery.

B.recommendation: Prioritize manually corrected failure cases from the student reader, especially unsupported answers with successful execution. Retain a smaller teacher-trace sample as a comparator.
B.baseline: Generate-and-filter teacher traces or the existing 35 verified trajectories without targeted correction.
B.matched_test: Use the review budget on 50 student failure cases and 50 teacher-generated traces from matched questions. Blind reviewers label executable validity, evidence location, support, and novel corrective action; replay each corrected trace. If later training is authorized, compare equal-size datasets on named held-out questions.
B.decision_rule: Favor corrected failures for the next dataset only if at least 10 more of 50 reviewed cases provide replay-valid, independently support-checked useful supervision than the matched teacher set. Training threshold is explicitly unset pending a held-out evaluation protocol.
B.uncertainty: The cited agent studies use web or tool benchmarks and different teachers; manual correction quality and time per case are unmeasured. A near-miss in those studies may differ from a paper-QA support failure.

claims.text: PROOF-Gen reports that generate-and-filter teacher data discards hard failed scenarios and proposes recovering passing traces from failures.
The SRC study uses bounded teacher review to locate harmful deviations in student agent branches.
